title: Using a Self-Assessment as a Team Exercise
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article proposes using self-assessment surveys as a group discussion tool rather than purely an individual development instrument. Having every team member complete the same assessment and share results surfaces patterns worth exploring together, such as why certain traits cluster across the group or what factors are propelling or blocking the team. The author walks through Angela Duckworth's Grit survey as a worked example, noting how reviewing individual items sparks conversation about which factors matter most to the team. The piece lists several other popular tools, including Google's Team Effectiveness Survey and Gallup's Q12, and stresses that the leader, not a facilitator, should choose which quality is worth examining. It closes with the observation that these assessments matter less for their objective accuracy than for the quality of reflection they provoke.
points: Self-assessment surveys can double as a structured team discussion exercise, not just individual insight
Group patterns in results raise natural questions worth exploring together as a team
Angela Duckworth's Grit survey is offered as a worked example of the exercise
The leader, not a facilitator, should choose which quality or tool is worth the team's discussion time
quotes: Beyond what leaders can learn about themselves from self-assessment tools, surveys can also serve as an ideal catalyst for team discussion and group insight.
Patterns in the results that emerge across the group are a strong place to start the conversation.
Take, for example, the self-assessment of Grit. Psychologist Angela Duckworth has written extensively about the concept of Grit.
Selecting an assessment that measures a quality worth discussing is critically important.
Good leaders recognize that the real power of these assessments is not to accurately reflect reality.
Through quality discussion, good assessments reveal the reality of the team’s reflection.
